_about: Data behind the atlas plates (ktatlas.py). Every event and every source carries a `source` line saying where the fact was read; ktatlascheck.py refuses an entry without one. Region rings are hand-placed approximations and the plates say so. Coordinates are lon, lat. Read dates are 2026-09-23 unless stated.

regions_1593.name: HABSBURG LANDS
regions_1593.source: The frontier of 1593 drawn by hand from the fortress lines: Kanizsa (Ottoman 1600), Gyor (Ottoman 1594-98), Komarom, Esztergom (Ottoman 1543-95), Fulek and Nograd (Ottoman to 1593), Eger (Ottoman 1596), Tokaj and Kassa (Royal). Approximate. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Turkish_War; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Hungary

regions_1593.name: OTTOMAN HUNGARY
regions_1593.source: Same construction; the Ottoman side of the same fortress line. Approximate.

regions_1593.name: TRANSYLVANIA
regions_1593.source: The principality with the Partium (Bihar, Szatmar, Maramaros) as it stood before the 1594-95 alliance with the Habsburgs. Approximate. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principality_of_Transylvania_(1570%E2%80%931711)

regions_1593.name: VENICE
regions_1593.source: Venetian Istria and Dalmatia, the coast only. Approximate.

events.label: The paper is made
events.desc: The paper the codex is written on is reported to be Venetian, made in the 1530s. The watermark study is cited at second hand and this edition has not seen it.
events.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rohonc_Codex: 'Study of the paper on which the codex is written shows that it is most probably a Venetian paper made in the 1530s.' Read 2026-09-23.

events.label: The proposed reading gives 1593
events.desc: On Király and Tokai's reading, one of the last leaves counts one thousand five hundred and sixty years from the Ascension, giving 1593. That summer the Long Turkish War began. Where in Hungary the codex was written, and by whom, is not known.
events.source: The book, introduction and the endnote on 223v; Király and Tokai 2018; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Turkish_War (1593-1606).

events.label: A catalogue entry, perhaps
events.desc: A 1743 catalogue of the Batthyany library at Rohonc lists 'Magyar imadsagok, volumen I in 12' -- Hungarian prayers, one small volume. It may or may not be the codex.
events.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rohonc_Codex and hu.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rohonci_kodex, both read 2026-09-23; both say the identification is uncertain.

events.label: To the Academy
events.desc: Count Gusztav Batthyany gives his library at Rohonc, some 30,000 volumes, to the Hungarian Academy of Sciences. The codex is in it and takes the town's name. Most accounts say 1838; the Hungarian article on the town says 1839.
events.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rohonc_Codex (1838); hu.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rohonc: '30 000 kotetes konyvtarat 1839-ben Batthyany Gusztav a Magyar Tudomanyos Akademianak ajandekozta.'

events.label: Toldy looks first
events.desc: Ferenc Toldy is the first scholar to study it. Pal Hunfalvy follows; neither reads a word.

events.label: Called a forgery
events.desc: Karoly Szabo proposes that the codex is a hoax by Samuel Literati Nemes, a known forger of antiquities. The charge stands in the literature for a century and a half.

events.label: Jirecek and Julg give up
events.desc: Josef and Konstantin Jirecek, then Bernhard Julg at Innsbruck, examine it and find nothing they can read.

events.label: Nemati counts 792 signs
events.desc: Kalman Nemati counts the distinct signs and finds 792 -- far too many for an alphabet, which is the first real fact about the script.

events.label: Rohonc passes into Austria
events.desc: Burgenland passes from Hungary to Austria. Rechnitz, an older German name for the town, is again official; its Hungarian name remains Rohonc. The codex itself stays in Budapest.
events.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rechnitz: the German name was in use centuries before 1921; the Hungarian name was made official in 1898; the town joined Austrian Burgenland in 1921.

events.label: Gyurk: right to left, and numbers
events.desc: Otto Gyurk shows the writing runs right to left and finds the numbers. His observation that the repeated sequences break at the line is the one this edition's whole reading rests on.
events.source: Otto Gyurk, 'Megfejtheto-e a Rohonci-kodex?', Elet es Tudomany 25 (1970), 1923-1928, cited in the book's Acknowledgment; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rohonc_Codex.

events.label: Locsmandi: not gibberish
events.desc: Miklos Locsmandi runs the text through a computer and rejects the idea that it is meaningless filler.

events.label: Nyiri: Sumerian
events.desc: Attila Nyiri reads it as Sumerian ligatures. Dismissed at once.

events.label: Enachiuc: Dacian
events.desc: Viorica Enachiuc publishes a reading as a Daco-Romanian dialect of Vulgar Latin, a history of the Vlachs in the eleventh and twelfth centuries, read right to left and bottom to top. Rejected.

events.label: Singh: Brahmi
events.desc: Mahesh Kumar Singh reads it as a variant of Brahmi carrying an apocryphal gospel, left to right. Rejected.

events.label: Láng: a cipher, not a hoax
events.desc: Benedek Láng argues the codex is a consciously encoded text and not a forgery, and writes the history of the problem (A Rohonci kód, 2011; in English as The Rohonc Code, 2021).
events.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rohonc_Codex; the book's Acknowledgment (Penn State Press, 2021).

events.label: Tokai and Király begin
events.desc: Gábor Tokai identifies the codes for the evangelists and reads the year numbers as Anno Mundi; Levente Zoltán Király works out the chapter structure and a table of contents.

events.label: An open transcription
events.desc: An anonymous author publishes a free, glyph-by-glyph transcription of the whole codex, in an alphabet of their own. It is the independent check this edition's tests lean on.
events.source: DATA_PROVENANCE.md section 1: revision 2.5, 2014-09-18, recovered from the Internet Archive.

events.label: Király and Tokai read it
events.desc: Cracking the code of the Rohonc Codex, in Cryptologia: a code system rather than a cipher, 841 dictionary codes glossed in this edition's merged data, the proposed date 1593, and the content a Catholic reader of its time. The dictionary this edition stands on.

events.label: Király on its theology
events.desc: Király's paper on the theological character of the codex, with the transcription and dictionary put online at rechnitzer-kodex.hu so the claims can be checked.
events.source: DATA_PROVENANCE.md section 2: A Rohonci kodex teologiai karaktere, in Hagyomany, Identitas, Tortenelem 2022 (publ. 2023).

events.label: This edition
events.desc: All 441 written pages rendered into English end to end, every word marked for how well it is known, with the tests and the data published beside it.

texts.name: The Gospels and Acts
texts.map_note: Not plotted: these books have different and, in several cases, disputed places of composition.
texts.line: the Passion, the parables, the Acts
texts.desc: The codex says its Passion is taken from Matthew and John, and most of its pages retell the gospels of the year. The compiler had them in the Vulgate.
texts.source: The book, introduction; the corpus appendix (Douay-Rheims, Gutenberg 8300).

texts.name: Josephus, The Wars of the Jews
texts.desc: Written in Rome after the war. The codex tells the siege, Vespasian and Titus, and the mother who eats her child.

texts.name: The Life of Adam and Eve
texts.map_note: Not plotted: its date and place of origin are disputed.
texts.line: Adam, Eve, Seth and the branch
texts.desc: A Jewish and Christian textual tradition preserved in Greek, Latin and other versions; its precise date and place of origin are disputed. The codex opens with it and runs it straight into the legend of the Rood.
texts.source: The corpus appendix (Charles 1913, vol. 2); scholarship summarized by the NASSCAL e-Clavis, 'Life of Adam and Eve.'

texts.name: The Protevangelium of James
texts.map_note: Not plotted: its place of composition is not securely known.
texts.desc: The infancy gospel behind the Joachim and Anne cycle; its place of composition is debated. Pseudo-Matthew (probably 7th c., Latin) adds the Golden Gate.

texts.name: Tertullian, Adversus Praxean
texts.line: sun, ray and the ray's tip
texts.desc: The figure of the sun for the three Persons, in the endnotes.

texts.name: The Apocalypse of Elijah
texts.map_note: Not plotted: it is Egyptian, but Alexandria is not a secure place of composition.
texts.line: Elijah addressed by the word of the Lord
texts.desc: Egyptian and surviving in Coptic, commonly understood as a third-century core with fourth-century Christian reworking. Enoch and Elijah are killed by the Antichrist and raised after three days and a half.
texts.source: DATA_PROVENANCE.md section 6; David Frankfurter, Elijah in Upper Egypt (1993).

texts.name: Augustine, Quaestiones Evangeliorum
texts.desc: The two pence as the two commandments of love, in the endnotes.

texts.name: The Reversio sanctae crucis
texts.map_note: Not plotted: its place of composition is not settled.
texts.desc: The Latin legend of Heraclius humbled at the gate of Jerusalem, dated between the end of the seventh century and the middle of the eighth. Where it was written is not settled.

texts.name: Adso, On the Antichrist
texts.desc: Montier-en-Der, Champagne.

texts.name: Barlaam and Ioasaph
texts.line: the apologue of the man in the well
texts.desc: Greek, attributed to St John Damascene; the version behind the Latin ones is from Mount Athos around the year 1000.
texts.source: The corpus appendix (Woodward and Mattingly, Gutenberg 749).

texts.name: Michael and Satanael
texts.line: the stolen robe, wreath and sceptre
texts.desc: A Bulgarian apocryphon: Satanael sets up a throne of his own; Gabriel is sent and refuses, then Michael. The nearest cousin to the codex's Lucifer pages.

texts.name: The Slavonic Book of Enoch
texts.desc: Survives whole only in Church Slavonic, over twenty manuscripts; Coptic fragments exist. Its date of composition is disputed.

texts.name: Voragine, the Golden Legend
texts.line: the Rood, the Finding of the Cross, the saints
texts.desc: The great Latin legendary. The compiler had it in Latin; this edition reads it in Caxton's English.

texts.name: The Wartburgkrieg
texts.desc: Recorded as a trap: the Grail cup was added to the poem in 1832. The codex's cup has no medieval Grail behind it.

texts.name: The Debreceni codex
texts.line: Seth at Adam's grave, in Hungarian
texts.desc: Made for the Poor Clares at Obuda; kept in Debrecen since 1753. One of three Hungarian codices of the 1520s that carry the Seth episode.
texts.source: National Szechenyi Library, nyelvemlekek.oszk.hu/adatlap/debreceni_kodex; Lovas, 'Adam a kereszt alatt' (ELTE); DATA_PROVENANCE.md section 6.

texts.name: The Erdy codex
texts.line: the branch promised, the healing deferred
texts.desc: Probably written by the Carthusian associated with Lovold; the exact place of composition is not certain.

texts.name: The Teleki codex
texts.desc: The only telling named in the notes in which Adam is alive when Seth comes back, as the codex has it.

texts.name: Carion's Chronicle
texts.line: six thousand years, in three spans
texts.desc: Melanchthon's preface carries the scheme the codex's end-of-world count belongs to.

texts.name: The Council of Trent
texts.line: the water mixed with the wine
texts.desc: Session 22, chapter 7 and canon 9.

texts.name: The Roman Missal
texts.desc: A Catholic reader of 1593 is at least as much missal and breviary as it is scripture.
texts.source: The corpus appendix; DATA_PROVENANCE.md section 6; Vatican Library, Missale Romanum ex decreto sacrosancti Concilii Tridentini restitutum (1570).

texts.name: The Roman Martyrology
texts.desc: The official Roman edition was promulgated in 1584, not with the Missal in 1570.
texts.source: DATA_PROVENANCE.md section 6; Vatican, Martyrologium Romanum: the first editio typica was approved on 14 January 1584.

texts.name: Caxton's Golden Legend
texts.line: the English the Legend is read in here
texts.desc: Westminster. Also London: the King James Bible (1611), Whiston's Josephus (1737), Wake's apocryphal gospels (1820), the English Missal (1865).

texts.name: The York, Chester, Towneley and N-Town plays
texts.map_note: Not plotted: these are four distinct collections, and the origins of Towneley and N-Town are not securely fixed to one city.
texts.desc: Four distinct English dramatic collections, not a single York corpus; Towneley and N-Town cannot be securely pinned to one city.
texts.source: The corpus appendix; British Library collection guides for the York, Chester, Towneley and N-Town manuscripts.

texts.name: The Douay-Rheims Bible
texts.line: the Catholic English of the Vulgate
texts.desc: Challoner's revision (1750). The Bible this edition reads the codex against, because the compiler worked from the Vulgate.

texts.name: Suarez, De Angelis
texts.desc: Posthumous. Cited at second hand.

texts.name: Mary of Agreda, Mystical City of God
texts.desc: Too late to be a source; cited as a parallel.

texts.name: Kalmany's folk tellings
texts.line: Elijah at the fall of the angels
texts.desc: Villages near Szeged; restated by Balint (1978).

texts.name: The Romanian carols of Judas
texts.desc: Colinde collected in Wallachia and Transylvania: the little jug of wine, the throne, the sun and moon.

texts.name: Lovas on the Hungarian codices
texts.line: the Seth episode in three codices
texts.map_note: not plotted: a study of the codices, not a source of stories; the codices themselves are.

tongues.areas_source: Indicative, not surveyed: the broad distribution of the vernaculars of the Kingdom of Hungary and its neighbours around 1600, drawn by hand. German also in the towns of Upper Hungary and among the Transylvanian Saxons; Croat refugee villages in the west from the 1530s (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgenland_Croats: 'These areas were occupied by the Turks during the Turkish wars (1533-1584)'; hu.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rohonc: 1532, 'horvatokat telepitettek ide'); Romanian written in Cyrillic 1500s-1860s (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_Cyrillic_alphabet, Neacsu's letter 1521).
tongues.marks_source: Edict of Torda, 28 January 1568: Catholic, Lutheran, Calvinist and Unitarian received; the Orthodox tolerated but not received (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_of_Torda). The other confessional placings are the standard account: Lutheran among the Germans and the western and Saxon towns, Calvinist at Debrecen, Ottoman garrisons and mosques in the occupied towns (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestantism_in_Hungary; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Hungary).
tongues.presses_source: hu.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manlius_Janos, read 2026-09-23: Laibach 1575-81; from 1582 on the western Hungarian estates; Varasd 1587; Nemetlovo 1592 (Kozarvari); Sarvar 1602 (Magyari); died c. 1604-05 at Nemetkeresztur.
tongues.glyphs_source: Király and Tokai's dictionary, exact-gloss entries; the signs traced from the manuscript's ink (ktdeep.py).
